diagnosis: Chronic kidney disease from hypertension and diabetes

examinerBank.question: Walk me through your approach to this patient's renal impairment - what is your differential and how do you localise the cause?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: First confirm chronicity using the old creatinine values (140→180→410 over 2 years) rather than treating this as new AKI. Exclude post-renal obstruction with a bladder scan and ultrasound - both normal here. Assess volume status clinically, which shows overload. Then use urine dipstick/microscopy to localise: bland sediment with heavy proteinuria in a patient with 15 years of hypertension and 12 years of poorly controlled diabetes, plus small echogenic kidneys on ultrasound and hypertensive/diabetic retinopathy, points strongly to combined hypertensive nephrosclerosis and diabetic nephropathy as the primary chronic process. I would still screen for superimposed acute injury from the recent NSAID use and muthi enema, and exclude glomerulonephritis (no dysmorphic RBCs/casts), HIVAN (HIV negative, kidneys small not enlarged) and myeloma (screen negative) before settling on the diagnosis.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks: mentions chronicity confirmation, obstruction exclusion, volume assessment, urine microscopy localisation, and ranked differential with correct reasoning. Partial credit for jumping straight to diagnosis without systematic localisation.

examinerBank.question: Explain the pathophysiology of why this patient's kidneys are small and echogenic on ultrasound, and why this matters clinically.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Long-standing hypertension causes arteriolar hyalinosis and glomerulosclerosis (nephrosclerosis), while chronic hyperglycaemia causes glomerular hyperfiltration injury, mesangial expansion and glomerular basement membrane thickening (diabetic nephropathy). Both processes lead to progressive nephron loss, tubulointerstitial fibrosis and scarring, which manifests as reduced renal size and increased echogenicity with loss of corticomedullary differentiation on ultrasound. This matters because small kidneys confirm chronic, largely irreversible disease - distinguishing it from acute kidney injury where kidneys are typically normal or enlarged - and it also affects decisions like biopsy safety (relatively contraindicated in small kidneys) and prognosis.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants pathophysiological mechanism (arteriolosclerosis, hyperfiltration injury, fibrosis) plus clinical significance (chronicity marker, biopsy caveat), not just restating 'the kidneys are scarred.'

examinerBank.question: She mentions she's been taking ibuprofen and a traditional herbal enema. Why are you specifically worried about this combination in the context of her existing medications?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: She is on enalapril (an ACE-inhibitor) and likely has diuretic-like volume depletion from her declining renal function and possibly a diuretic on her chart - combined with the NSAID, this creates the classic 'triple whammy': NSAIDs block afferent arteriolar vasodilation (prostaglandin-mediated) while ACE-inhibitors block efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction (angiotensin II-mediated), both of which are compensatory mechanisms that maintain glomerular filtration pressure when renal perfusion is already compromised by chronic vascular disease. Removing both simultaneously in a volume-depleted or CKD state precipitates a predictable, preventable acute decline in GFR. The muthi enema adds further risk of direct nephrotoxicity and volume/electrolyte depletion, both well-documented causes of AKI-on-CKD in this region.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Must articulate the triple-whammy mechanism specifically (afferent vs efferent arteriolar effects) and connect it to this patient's regimen, plus recognise muthi nephrotoxicity as an additional local risk factor.

examinerBank.question: Recite the indications for urgent renal replacement therapy and tell me whether this patient meets any of them today.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: The mnemonic is AEIOU: refractory Acidosis, refractory hyperkalaemia (Electrolytes), dialysable Intoxication/overdose, refractory pulmonary Overload, and Uraemic complications such as encephalopathy, pericarditis or bleeding. Today she has bicarbonate 17 (mild acidosis, not refractory), potassium 5.6 (mild hyperkalaemia, no ECG changes, manageable medically for now), signs of volume overload with crackles and effusions but not yet refractory to diuretics, and no encephalopathy, pericardial rub or bleeding. So she does not meet urgent dialysis criteria today, but she is CKD stage 4 approaching stage 5 and needs nephrology referral for RRT planning and access creation before she becomes an emergency.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Must recite AEIOU correctly and apply each criterion to this specific patient's results, distinguishing 'needs dialysis today' from 'needs dialysis planning soon.'

framework: AKI vs CKD work-up applied to a patient found to have renal impairment: confirm chronicity (old creatinine, imaging), exclude reversible/post-renal causes, assess volume status, dipstick/microscopy urine, take drug history, localise cause, stage severity, plan RRT-readiness and follow-up

patient.name: Thandiwe Mthembu
patient.personality: soft-spoken, stoic, tends to underplay her swelling and breathlessness, proud of 'managing' her own tablets
patient.openingLine: Doctor, my legs are so swollen now I can't even fit my shoes, and I feel so tired all the time.

presentingComplaint: progressive leg swelling, fatigue and reduced urine output over 3 months in a patient with known long-standing hypertension and diabetes

history.fact: Leg swelling started about 3 months ago, gradually creeping up from ankles to knees, now also has some puffiness around the eyes in the morning
Urine output has reduced - she used to pass urine often, now goes less frequently and in smaller amounts; no complete anuria
Has noticed her urine looks 'foamy' or 'bubbly' in the toilet bowl for several months
Profound tiredness and reduced energy for daily chores over the last 2-3 months, worse than before
Gets short of breath walking to the outside toilet, and now sleeps propped up on two pillows because lying flat makes her breathless
Poor appetite for the last month, feels nauseous most mornings, has vomited twice
Complains of generalised itching, especially at night, for the past few weeks
Diagnosed with high blood pressure about 15 years ago; admits she often runs out of her tablets and misses clinic visits because of transport costs from Nongoma

Diagnosed with 'sugar sickness' (type 2 diabetes) about 12 years ago; on metformin and glibenclamide, control has been poor with several HbA1c readings 'in the high numbers' according to her clinic card
Her clinic card shows a creatinine of 180 µmol/L about 8 months ago, and one from 2 years ago around 140 µmol/L - a gradual rise over years, not a sudden change
Takes amlodipine and enalapril for pressure, metformin and glibenclamide for sugar; recently started ibuprofen bought over the counter for knee pain, taking it most days for the last month
Also been taking a traditional herbal enema ('isihlambezo') given by a neighbour for 'cleaning the blood' over the past 2 months
Lives alone in a rural homestead near Nongoma, three children live in Durban, relies on her old-age grant; long distance and cost to reach clinic for follow-up
Never smoked; drinks alcohol occasionally at family gatherings, no regular use
Mother died of 'kidney trouble' in her 60s; father had a stroke; one sister also has sugar sickness
No haematuria, no colicky loin pain, no difficulty starting or stopping urine stream, no known pelvic mass or abnormal vaginal bleeding
Tested HIV negative two years ago at the clinic
No fever, no joint pains, no rash, no recent infections, no chest pain

examination.general: Chronically unwell-looking elderly woman, pale conjunctivae, mild bilateral pitting oedema to mid-shin, periorbital puffiness, scratch marks on forearms from itching, no clubbing, no cyanosis
examination.respiratory: Bibasal fine crackles on auscultation, reduced air entry at both lung bases consistent with small pleural effusions, no wheeze
examination.cardio: Displaced apex beat (left ventricular hypertrophy), JVP raised 4cm, soft systolic flow murmur, no pericardial rub
examination.abdo: Soft, non-tender, no palpable masses, no palpable bladder, no hepatosplenomegaly, no ascites
examination.neuro: Alert and oriented, no asterixis, no focal deficits, reduced vibration sense in both feet (peripheral neuropathy consistent with diabetes)

investigations.name: Urea & electrolytes/creatinine
investigations.result: Creatinine 410 µmol/L (baseline 140-180 µmol/L over 2 years), urea 22 mmol/L, potassium 5.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L

investigations.name: Renal tract ultrasound
investigations.result: Bilateral small, echogenic kidneys with reduced corticomedullary differentiation (right 8.2cm, left 8.0cm), no hydronephrosis, no obstruction

investigations.name: Urine dipstick and microscopy
investigations.result: Protein 3+, no blood, no leucocytes/nitrites; microscopy shows no cellular casts, no dysmorphic red cells - bland sediment consistent with chronic nephrosclerosis

investigations.name: Full blood count
investigations.result: Hb 8.9 g/dL normocytic normochromic (anaemia of CKD), WCC 6.8, platelets 240

investigations.name: Calcium, phosphate, PTH
investigations.result: Corrected calcium 2.05 mmol/L (low-normal), phosphate 1.9 mmol/L (raised), PTH 210 pg/mL (elevated, secondary hyperparathyroidism)

investigations.name: Serum/urine electrophoresis and free light chains
investigations.result: No monoclonal band, normal free light chain ratio - myeloma screen negative

investigations.name: ECG
investigations.result: Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern, no peaked T waves despite K 5.6

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Cardiomegaly, bilateral small pleural effusions, upper lobe venous diversion consistent with early pulmonary oedema

differentials.dx: Chronic kidney disease secondary to hypertensive nephrosclerosis and diabetic nephropathy
for: 12-year history of poorly controlled diabetes with HbA1c 9.8%
bilateral small echogenic kidneys on ultrasound
bland urine sediment with heavy proteinuria
hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy on fundoscopy

differentials.dx: Acute-on-chronic kidney injury (superimposed AKI from NSAID and/or muthi nephrotoxicity, or triple-whammy effect)
for: concurrent enalapril and likely diuretic effect creating triple-whammy risk
creatinine rise appears somewhat accelerated over recent months
against: ultrasound shows small kidneys typical of established chronic disease, not acute insult
no eosinophils/casts suggestive of interstitial nephritis on microscopy
gradual trajectory over years fits chronicity better than acute superimposed injury alone

differentials.dx: Glomerulonephritis (primary or secondary, e.g. lupus nephritis, IgA nephropathy)
against: bland urine sediment with no dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts
no systemic features (rash, joint pains, oral ulcers)
clear long-standing hypertension/diabetes history explains the picture better

for: nephrotic-range proteinuria common presentation in KZN
against: HIV test negative on two occasions
ultrasound typically shows large echogenic kidneys in HIVAN, not small kidneys as seen here

for: reduced urine output could suggest obstruction
against: normal post-void residual on bladder scan
no loin pain, haematuria or pelvic mass on history/exam

pathophys.peripheral and periorbital oedema: Reduced GFR causes sodium and water retention; nephrotic-range proteinuria lowers plasma oncotic pressure, favouring fluid shift into the interstitium; hypertension and heart strain compound venous pressure
pathophys.fatigue: Reduced erythropoietin production by diseased peritubular fibroblasts causes anaemia of CKD, compounded by uraemic toxin accumulation impairing cellular metabolism
pathophys.orthopnoea and breathlessness: Sodium/water retention and left ventricular hypertrophy from chronic hypertension reduce compliance and reserve, causing pulmonary venous congestion that worsens when lying flat due to increased venous return
pathophys.pruritus: Retained uraemic toxins, secondary hyperparathyroidism and calcium-phosphate deposition in the skin stimulate cutaneous nerve endings
pathophys.foamy urine: Glomerular basement membrane damage from chronic hyperfiltration injury (diabetic nephropathy) and hypertensive arteriolosclerosis increases permeability to albumin, which reduces urine surface tension and produces persistent foam
pathophys.small echogenic kidneys on ultrasound: Long-standing nephron loss from glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis leads to progressive parenchymal scarring, loss of corticomedullary differentiation and reduction in renal size — the classic ultrasound signature of chronicity
pathophys.secondary hyperparathyroidism (raised PT: Failing kidneys cannot excrete phosphate or activate vitamin D (1-alpha-hydroxylation), causing hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia, which drive compensatory parathyroid hormone secretion — the start of CKD-mineral bone disease

staging: CKD stage G4 (eGFR ~12 mL/min/1.73m² using MDRD, note eGFR equations less reliable at extremes) A3 (nephrotic-range albuminuria); NYHA class II-III symptoms from volume overload; poorly controlled T2DM (HbA1c 9.8%) and hypertension (178/104)

immediate: Stop nephrotoxic ibuprofen immediately and counsel against further NSAID use
Stop the traditional herbal enema and counsel sensitively about muthi nephrotoxicity risk
Assess and manage volume overload — cautious diuresis (furosemide) given pulmonary oedema signs, strict fluid balance
Check ECG and treat hyperkalaemia if it worsens (calcium gluconate, insulin-dextrose, salbutamol nebs) per SA EML/Adult STGs
Withhold/dose-adjust enalapril temporarily if creatinine rising acutely, reassess after volume status addressed
definitive: Optimise blood pressure control per CKD target (<130/80) with renally-appropriate agents, continue ACE-inhibitor at reduced dose once stable given proteinuria benefit, monitor potassium and creatinine closely after any dose change
Optimise glycaemic control with renally-adjusted regimen (avoid/reduce glibenclamide due to hypoglycaemia risk in CKD; consider insulin or renally-safe agents; stop metformin if eGFR <30)
Refer to nephrology for CKD stage 4 management and RRT planning/education (haemodialysis vs peritoneal dialysis vs conservative care discussion)
Start erythropoiesis-stimulating agent and iron replacement for renal anaemia if indicated
Manage CKD-mineral bone disease: phosphate binders, active vitamin D analogue, dietary phosphate restriction
supportive: Dietary counselling — salt restriction, protein moderation, phosphate/potassium awareness
Vaccination status review (hepatitis B given future dialysis access risk)
Arrange transport/social support given rural distance from Nongoma to clinic to prevent missed follow-up
Educate on avoiding NSAIDs and unregulated traditional remedies long-term
followUp: Recheck renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure within 1-2 weeks after diuretic initiation and NSAID cessation
Formal nephrology follow-up for CKD stage 4/5 trajectory and dialysis-access planning (AV fistula referral if progressing)
Medication reconciliation at every visit — this is a commonly missed discharge step
Regular HbA1c, lipid profile, and cardiovascular risk review
Home-based or clinic-based BP and glucose monitoring with community health worker support

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, explains purpose of consultation, gains consent
Actively seeks an old/baseline creatinine value or clinic card history to distinguish AKI from CKD
stationChecklist.answer: Clinic card shows creatinine 140 µmol/L 2 years ago, 180 µmol/L 8 months ago, now 410 µmol/L - gradual chronic rise
stationChecklist.why: Old creatinine is the single most useful discriminator between AKI and CKD

stationChecklist.item: Establishes duration and control of hypertension and diabetes, including adherence and clinic attendance
stationChecklist.answer: 15 years hypertension, 12 years diabetes, poor control, erratic tablet supply and missed follow-up due to transport cost
stationChecklist.why: Identifies the two driving chronic diseases for this case's diagnosis

stationChecklist.item: Screens for volume overload symptoms (oedema, orthopnoea, reduced urine output) and uraemic symptoms (itch, nausea, fatigue)
stationChecklist.answer: Progressive leg/periorbital oedema, orthopnoea on 2 pillows, reduced urine volume, pruritus, nausea, fatigue
stationChecklist.why: Defines clinical syndrome and urgency of fluid management

stationChecklist.item: Takes full drug history including OTC NSAIDs, ACEi/diuretic combination, and specifically asks about traditional medicine/muthi/enemas
stationChecklist.answer: Recent ibuprofen use, on enalapril, and traditional herbal enema (isihlambezo) for 2 months
stationChecklist.why: Identifies reversible/superimposed nephrotoxic contributors and the classic KZN muthi nephrotoxicity and triple-whammy traps

stationChecklist.item: Screens for obstructive/post-renal symptoms (stream, haematuria, loin pain, pelvic mass/bleeding)
stationChecklist.answer: No obstructive symptoms, no haematuria, no loin pain, no pelvic mass/bleeding
stationChecklist.why: Post-renal obstruction must never be missed - even when history points to chronicity, must be actively excluded

stationChecklist.item: Performs focused volume status examination (JVP, lung bases, oedema, BP) before deciding fluid management
stationChecklist.answer: Raised JVP, bibasal crackles, pitting oedema, BP 178/104 - fluid overloaded and hypertensive
stationChecklist.why: Volume assessment is the pivotal exam step dictating fluid management direction

stationChecklist.item: Performs or requests bladder scan to exclude obstruction
stationChecklist.why: 30-second bedside test that must never be omitted in any renal impairment work-up

stationChecklist.item: Examines for signs of uraemia (asterixis, pericardial rub) and end-organ damage (fundoscopy for retinopathy, peripheral neuropathy)
stationChecklist.answer: No asterixis or rub; retinopathy and peripheral neuropathy present, consistent with long-standing hypertension/diabetes
stationChecklist.why: Confirms chronic end-organ damage pattern and screens for dialysis-urgency signs

stationChecklist.item: Offers ranked differential distinguishing chronic hypertensive/diabetic nephropathy from superimposed AKI, glomerulonephritis, HIVAN and obstruction, with reasoning
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning with anatomical localisation is the exam philosophy

stationChecklist.item: Requests and correctly interprets urine dipstick/microscopy (bland sediment vs casts) to support chronic nephrosclerosis over active glomerular disease
stationChecklist.answer: 3+ protein, bland sediment, no cellular casts or dysmorphic RBCs - supports chronic nephrosclerosis rather than active GN
stationChecklist.why: Urine microscopy table is exam-central for localising renal pathology

stationChecklist.item: Requests renal tract ultrasound to assess kidney size/echogenicity and confirm chronicity, excluding obstruction
stationChecklist.answer: Bilateral small echogenic kidneys, no hydronephrosis
stationChecklist.why: Kidney size on ultrasound is a key chronicity marker; also excludes obstruction

stationChecklist.item: Considers/sends myeloma screen (serum/urine electrophoresis, free light chains) given unexplained renal impairment in a patient over 40
stationChecklist.answer: Electrophoresis and free light chains sent, negative for monoclonal disease
stationChecklist.why: Explicitly flagged as a mandatory screen in any unexplained AKI/CKD over 40 years

stationChecklist.item: Recognises that eGFR/creatinine trend (not a single calculated eGFR) is used to judge severity, and correctly stages CKD
stationChecklist.answer: Trended creatinine over 2 years shows chronic progressive decline; staged as CKD G4 A3
stationChecklist.why: eGFR equations and single creatinine values can mislead; trend and staging emphasised repeatedly

stationChecklist.item: Outlines immediate management (stop NSAID/muthi, treat volume overload, correct hyperkalaemia if present) and definitive management (BP/glucose optimisation, nephrology referral, RRT planning)
stationChecklist.why: Comprehensive stepwise management per SA guidelines from immediate stabilisation through to dialysis planning

stationChecklist.item: Explicitly plans follow-up: renal function/BP recheck, medication reconciliation, nephrology referral, and addresses transport/access barriers
stationChecklist.why: Discharge follow-up and medication review is flagged as one of the commonest omissions
